articles.title: Docker failed to solve: rpc error: code = Canceled in CI
articles.excerpt: Docker failed to solve: rpc error: code = Canceled is not a fault report. It is BuildKit relaying that the call carrying your build was canceled, in wording that comes from gRPC and from the Go standa…
articles.body: Docker failed to solve: rpc error: code = Canceled is not a fault report. It is BuildKit relaying that the call carrying your build was canceled, in wording that comes from gRPC and from the Go standard library rather than from Docker, and the only useful question is which program did the canceling. The words "rpc error: code = Canceled desc =" are formatted by gRPC and "context canceled" by the Go standard library. Only "failed to solve" belongs to Docker tooling. What this error means A build that was making progress stops partway. One step shows as CANCELED rather than as an error, and the job ends with a solve failure carrying a gRPC code and the words context canceled. No step reported a problem of its own, and rerunning the same commit frequently succeeds.
articles.author: Kay

articles.title: USDT on Tron and the energy bill: what sweeping TRC-20 deposits really costs
articles.excerpt: If you take stablecoins, a lot of your customers will want to pay in USDT on Tron. Transfers are cheap for them and most exchanges support withdrawals on it. Then you build the part that moves those d…
articles.body: If you take stablecoins, a lot of your customers will want to pay in USDT on Tron. Transfers are cheap for them and most exchanges support withdrawals on it. Then you build the part that moves those deposits somewhere safe, and you find out the cheap part was only cheap for the sender. This post is about that second step: getting USDT out of per-customer deposit addresses and into a wallet you control, and why the cost of doing it on Tron behaves differently from what you might expect if you've only done this on EVM chains. Two resources, not one gas price On Ethereum-style chains you think in gas: a transaction uses some units, you pay a price per unit, done. Tron splits the cost into two resources: Bandwidth , which pays for the bytes of the transaction.

articles.title: A2UI Protocol: How Agents Stream Layout Data Instead of HTML to Native UI Components
articles.excerpt: Most agent UIs stream markdown or generate HTML strings. A2UI streams layout data that native framework adapters translate into platform components. The agent emits structured events describing button…
articles.body: Most agent UIs stream markdown or generate HTML strings. A2UI streams layout data that native framework adapters translate into platform components. The agent emits structured events describing buttons, cards, and forms. The client renders them using React, Flutter, SwiftUI, or Jetpack Compose without a WebView or eval(). This separation creates strict capability boundaries. The agent cannot inject arbitrary code. It composes from a fixed catalog of components defined by the application. The protocol is event-based and optimized for low-latency streaming, making it viable for real-time agent interactions across web and mobile platforms. Why Layout Data Instead of Code Generative UI typically means an LLM writes JSX or HTML, then the client renders it.

articles.title: Metal Sandbox: Isolated Execution and Command Scheduling for GPU Coding Agents on Apple Silicon
articles.excerpt: Agents that generate GPU kernels need to compile, test, and iterate on Metal code without monopolizing the host GPU or crashing when concurrent sessions compete for command queues. Metal Sandbox addre…
articles.body: Agents that generate GPU kernels need to compile, test, and iterate on Metal code without monopolizing the host GPU or crashing when concurrent sessions compete for command queues. Metal Sandbox addresses this by isolating file workspaces, scheduling command execution across a pool of Apple Silicon nodes, and migrating eligible commands to idle machines when local capacity is saturated. The paper (arXiv 2611.17294v1) reports 1.68× to 2.05× command throughput gains on four Mac mini M4 nodes under concentrated demand, and 22.3% reductions in batch elapsed time when dynamic scheduling replaces static assignment. The Problem: GPU Resource Contention in Agent Loops A typical GPU coding agent alternates between three phases: Model inference to generate candidate kernel code.

articles.title: err_pnpm_fetch_503 and the rest of the pnpm fetch codes
articles.excerpt: The code err_pnpm_fetch_503 is pnpm telling you the registry answered your request and refused it, and the number on the end is the HTTP status, not a pnpm error catalog entry. That is why the family…
articles.body: The code err_pnpm_fetch_503 is pnpm telling you the registry answered your request and refused it, and the number on the end is the HTTP status, not a pnpm error catalog entry. That is why the family is open ended: any status pnpm does not like becomes a code with that status in the name, and the one you get determines whether retrying is sensible or pointless. The number in the code is the HTTP status. Everything useful follows from that: whether pnpm retried, whether retrying again would help, and which setting is the one to move. What this error means The install fails during resolution, before anything is linked, on one package. Older pnpm prints two warnings about retrying and then a line beginning with the code, the HTTP method, the URL, the reason phrase and the status.

The median VPS with the same memory costs $336, and the median 64 GB plan at the four big clouds costs $504. Those are medians from our price snapshot of 15 November 2026, taken across 553 VPS plans from 40 hosts and 204 dedicated servers from 18. A dedicated server is a whole physical machine rented to one customer, often called bare metal. A VPS is a slice of a shared machine. The guides that rank for this question give a fixed point to switch at: Valebyte says 8 busy vCPUs and 32 GB or more, Atlantic.Net says customers tend to move at 32 to 48 GB, and Worldstream uses 70% utilization. None of them prices it.

articles.title: Bluetooth HDT could finally fix wireless audio quality, but there’s still one big problem
articles.excerpt: HDT will be one of the biggest changes to Bluetooth audio in years.
articles.body: News that Bluetooth has officially adopted its new High Data Throughput (HDT) specification should be music to audiophile ears far and wide. And there’s a good chance your future pair of wireless headphones could sound considerably better as a result. If you missed the announcement, Bluetooth HDT extends the capabilities of Bluetooth Low Energy (LE), boosting its maximum physical-layer data rate (PHY, pronounced “fie”) from 2Mbps to a comparatively colossal 7.5Mbps. That’s almost four times the maximum rate of conventional Bluetooth LE, and 2.5 times faster than Bluetooth Enhanced Data Rate (EDR), which tops out at 3Mbps.

articles.body: On Episode 236 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Mikhail Tikhonov to talk about how life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. When we think of extraterrestrials, our minds generally go from the latex-suited bipedal aliens seen in Star Trek and Star Wars to more exotic critters in sci-fi movies. Scientists think in terms of carbon-based microbial life and other lower life forms. But some researchers, such as Tikhonov from Washington University, suggest that life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. He further suggests a new definition of life: something that takes in and transforms energy and replicates. His ideas radically expand our notions of alien life and how it might be recognized.

articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman . That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely .

articles.body: Update for 3:40 p.m. ET on Nov. 14: SpaceX's Kate Tice provided more information about the booster abort at about 3:30 p.m. EST (1830 GMT) on Nov. 14, during the company's Flight 15 webcast. "Early indications are that the booster ended its boostback [burn] early due to a low fuel mass alarm," she said. "The team is still investigating the root cause on that." SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13), triggering an automatic abort that destroyed the booster. The giant Starship rocket , a massive two-stage vehicle that's the largest launcher on Earth, soared into orbit from SpaceX's Starbase in South Texas on Friday on the company's ambitious Flight 15 test flight.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 astronauts launched to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier.
